newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore's small opposition turns to wide issues.
newsitem.headline: Singapore's small opposition turns to wide issues.

text.p: Singapore's opposition parties are turning to larger national issues rather than local concerns in their attempts to win a bigger voice in government in this week's general election.
The ruling People's Action Party (PAP) is calling on voters in Thursday's poll to consider who is best placed to deliver government benefits to individual constituencies.
Opposition parties decry such PAP tactics such as linking upgrading of public housing to how constitencies vote. They say that unfairly excludes their wards from a taxpayer-funded national programme.
"If voters base their vote just on upgrading, that would be a tragedy," Low Thia Kiang of the Workers' Party said at a news conference.

He took a swipe at his PAP opponent's analogy that candidates were like rival contractors vying for the voters' contract. "I am not a contractor. I am a candidate standing for election as a representative of the people," Low said.
The fractured opposition -- five parties are fighting the PAP -- have been urging the electorate to stand by broad principles in the face of PAP appeals to pragmatism.
Singapore Democratic Party chief Chee Soon Juan said his party would not allow the PAP to "hijack" the election.
"We want the basic freedoms, to have the right to question our government, to have it be accountable to us, to have a say in how our country is run," Chee said in an interview.
Other opposition parties are highlighting the cost of living, including rising health-care costs, and the need for an alternative voice in parliament.
The National Solidarity Party (NSP) has stressed its concern about what it says is a growing gap between rich and poor.

NSP candidate Wong Wee Nam, a family doctor, said he was against policies such as the wage formula that has given Singapore ministers some of the highest salaries of any of the world's government officials.
This gave undue emphasis to the elite in society, he said.
Even if Wong and every other opposition candidate were to win, they would have an uphill battle implementing their ideas.
The PAP is already assured of a parliamentary majority, as its candidates are unopposed in 47 of the 83 seats.

Some opposition leaders, like the SDP's Chee, see that as a plus since they believe many Singaporeans are not yet ready for a change of government but want more opposition members in parliament as a check on the PAP.
This line of thinking holds that such citizens will vote for opposition candidates if assured the PAP will stay in power.

The PAP has held power since independence from Britain in 1959. Even many critics credit its economic policies for helping make Singapore one of the richest countries in Asia, with an average per capita income ahead of many European nations.
In the last election, in 1991, the PAP won all but four of 81 parliamentary seats.

But that was the opposition's highest tally since independence, and opposition parties say Singapore is ready for a less heavyhanded, more liberal approach, and one that does more for the bottom strata of society.
However, even some opposition figures would consider it a major achievement to increase their seats from four to 10, and neutral analysts think they may be lucky to keep what they have.
